Let’s dive into Chapter 5: Common Games and Their Impact on Relationships.
You know, psychological games show up in all sorts of ways. Some are pretty subtle, others are right out in the open. But there’s one thing they almost always have in common—they repeat, again and again, leaving everyone involved feeling stuck or just plain unsatisfied.
So, why do some relationships feel so challenging or even draining? Well, let’s look at a few of the most common games people play—maybe you’ll recognize one or two.
First up, there’s the classic “Why Don’t You—Yes But” game. Picture this: someone shares a problem and asks for advice. You offer a suggestion, but they immediately shoot it down. You try again, and again, every idea gets a “yes, but…” response. Sound familiar? The person asking gets attention and sympathy, but never has to actually change anything. Meanwhile, everyone else just gets frustrated.
Then there’s “If It Weren’t For You.” In this one, someone blames someone else—or maybe just the situation—for why they aren’t happy or fulfilled. Like when a partner says, “If it weren’t for you, I could have gone after my dreams.” At its core, it’s really about avoiding personal risks or fears. The payoff? They get to feel justified in not taking action.
Another one you might spot, especially at work or in families, is “Now I’ve Got You, You Son of a Gun.” This is where someone waits for another person to slip up—then pounces with criticism or blame. It creates a lot of tension and mistrust, but gives the person a sense of control or righteousness.
Some games are even sneakier, like “See What You Made Me Do.” Here, someone blames others for their own mistakes. It’s a way to dodge responsibility and maybe even get a little sympathy along the way. The real payoff? They don’t have to feel guilty or blame themselves.
The thing is, these games aren’t limited to just romantic partners or families. They show up between friends, coworkers, and even total strangers. Why do they keep happening? Because, at a deeper level, they meet certain emotional needs—like wanting attention, validation, or a sense of control.
Over time, though, these games take a toll. They create cycles of frustration, resentment, and misunderstanding. Trust and real connection start to wear away, making it tough to build the kind of relationships we really want.
But here’s the good news: once you spot these patterns, you can begin to change them. So, how do you break free?
First, refuse to play. When you notice a familiar script starting, make a different choice. Set clear boundaries—let others know your limits and what you expect. Stay focused on what’s actually happening now, instead of dragging in the past or what-ifs. And encourage responsibility; support the people around you in owning their choices.
When you understand the scripts and motives behind these common games, you open the door to transforming your relationships. Suddenly, there’s space for honesty, directness, and real fulfillment.
